slides.narration: A cricket ball, the Moon and a satellite launched from Sriharikota all obey one law of attraction. In this part we start from the way planets move round the Sun, meet Newton’s law of gravitation, add up the pulls of several masses, and then see how the acceleration due to gravity changes with height and depth.

slides.heading: Kepler’s three laws
slides.body_md: Kepler summarised the motion of the planets in three laws:
bullets: **Law of orbits:** every planet moves in an **ellipse** with the Sun at one **focus**.
**Law of areas:** the line from the Sun to the planet sweeps out **equal areas in equal times**.
**Law of periods:** the square of the period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis, $T^2 \propto a^3$.
The point of the orbit nearest the Sun is **perihelion**, the farthest is **aphelion**.

rows: A planet moves in an ellipse with the Sun at one focus
The line from Sun to planet sweeps equal areas in equal times
Force along the line: angular momentum is constant
T² is proportional to a³ (a = semi-major axis)

visual.alt: Table of Kepler three laws, what each states and its physical reason

slides.narration: Kepler found three rules in the observations of the planets. First, each orbit is an ellipse with the Sun at one focus. Second, the line joining the Sun and the planet sweeps equal areas in equal times. Third, the square of the period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis. The nearest point to the Sun is called perihelion and the farthest point aphelion.

slides.heading: The law of areas: fast near the Sun, slow far away
slides.body_md: In the picture the two wedges are swept in the same time interval.
bullets: Equal areas in equal times means the planet moves **faster near perihelion** and slower near aphelion.
The area swept per second is $\dfrac{dA}{dt} = \dfrac{L}{2m}$, where $L$ is the angular momentum about the Sun.
Gravity acts along the line to the Sun, so its torque about the Sun is zero and L stays constant.
At the two extreme points $v_p r_p = v_a r_a$, so the speed ratio is the inverse of the distance ratio.

slides.narration: Look at the two shaded wedges. They are swept in the same time, so they have the same area. The wedge near the Sun is short and wide, so the planet must cover a long arc, and it moves quickly. The wedge far from the Sun is long and thin, so the arc is short and the planet is slow. This is conservation of angular momentum, because gravity pulls straight towards the Sun.

slides.heading: The law of periods
slides.body_md: For orbits of different size around the same Sun, $\dfrac{T^2}{a^3}$ is the same constant.
bullets: In years and astronomical units (AU) the constant is 1 for the Sun: T² = a³.
A larger orbit has a longer period, and disproportionately so: double the radius, period × 2√2.
The table shows six planets; T²/a³ is 1.00 within the accuracy of the data.
Circular orbit: set $\dfrac{G M m}{r^2} = m \omega^2 r$ with $\omega = \dfrac{2\pi}{T}$ to get the formula above.

functions.label: T² = a³ (T in years, a in AU)

visual.alt: Plot of the square of the orbital period in years against the cube of the mean distance in astronomical units for the six inner planets: the points lie on the straight line through the origin with slope one
visual.caption: T² is proportional to a³: all planets lie on one straight line.

math: T^2 = \dfrac{4\pi^2}{G M}\, r^3 \quad \text{(circular orbit of radius } r\text{)}
slides.narration: The law of periods says that the square of the period divided by the cube of the mean distance is the same for every planet. Measure the period in years and the distance in astronomical units, and the constant for the Sun is exactly one. The graph shows all six inner planets falling on a single straight line. For a circular orbit you can derive the law by equating the gravitational force to the mass times omega squared times radius.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a small body far from the Sun
slides.body_md: A small body orbits the Sun at a mean distance of $2.25$ AU. Using Earth ($T = 1$ year at $1$ AU), find its period.
bullets: $\dfrac{T^2}{a^3}$ is the same for both: $\dfrac{T^2}{2.25^3} = \dfrac{1^2}{1^3}$.
Note: $T = a^{3/2} = 2.25^{1.5}$; the body takes 3.375 times as long as Earth.

functions.label: T² = a³ (T in years, a in AU)

visual.caption: T² is proportional to a³: all planets lie on one straight line.

slides.narration: Compare with Earth, whose period is one year at one astronomical unit. The ratio of period squared to distance cubed must be one for the small body too. The distance cubed is 11.391, so the period squared is the same number, and the period is 3.375 years.

slides.heading: Newton’s universal law of gravitation
slides.body_md: Every particle attracts every other particle with a force along the line joining them:
bullets: The force is **always attractive**, **mutual** (equal and opposite on the two bodies) and acts along the line joining them.
It varies as 1/r²: double the distance and the force falls to one quarter.
G is a universal constant, the same everywhere; it is so small that gravity between everyday objects is negligible.
A uniform sphere attracts outside bodies as if all its mass were at its centre.

slides.narration: Newton’s law says that two point masses attract with a force proportional to the product of the masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. The force acts along the line joining them, it is always attractive, and the two bodies pull on each other with equal and opposite forces. The constant G is very small, about six point six seven times ten to the power minus eleven in SI units, so the pull between everyday objects is tiny.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: the Sun pulls the Earth
slides.body_md: Take $M_S = 2.0 \times 10^{30}$ kg, $M_E = 6.0 \times 10^{24}$ kg and the Sun–Earth distance $1.5 \times 10^{11}$ m. Find the force of attraction.
bullets: $F = \dfrac{G M_S M_E}{r^2} = \dfrac{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 2.0 \times 10^{30} \times 6.0 \times 10^{24}}{(1.5 \times 10^{11})^2}$
The same force acts on the Sun (Newton’s third law), but the Sun’s acceleration is tiny because its mass is huge.

slides.heading: Superposition: the pull of several masses
slides.body_md: The force on a body due to several masses is the **vector sum** of the individual forces; each pair acts as if the others were absent.
bullets: $\vec F = \vec F_1 + \vec F_2 + \dots$, each $F_i = \dfrac{G m M_i}{r_i^2}$ directed towards mass $M_i$.
Draw each force along its line, then add the vectors by components or with the parallelogram law.
Forces from two equal masses on opposite sides of a body cancel on the line between them: there is a point of zero net force.
Sum for a few masses; for a uniform sphere the sum reduces to a single force at the centre.

slides.narration: Gravity obeys superposition. To find the force on one body from several others, work out the pull of each one separately, along its own line, and then add the forces as vectors. If two equal masses lie on opposite sides of a body, their pulls point opposite ways and cancel on the line between them.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: pulls at right angles
slides.body_md: A $4$ kg mass A has a $2$ kg mass B at $0.3$ m along $+x$ and a $3$ kg mass C at $0.4$ m along $+y$. Find the net gravitational force on A.
bullets: $F_{AB} = \dfrac{G m_A m_B}{r_B^2} = \dfrac{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 4 \times 2}{0.3^2} = 5.93 \times 10^{-9}$ N, along $+x$.
$F_{AC} = \dfrac{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 4 \times 3}{0.4^2} = 5.00 \times 10^{-9}$ N, along $+y$.
The forces are perpendicular: $F = \sqrt{F_{AB}^2 + F_{AC}^2} = 7.76 \times 10^{-9}$ N.
Direction: $\tan\theta = \dfrac{F_{AC}}{F_{AB}} = 0.844$, so $\theta \approx 40.2^\circ$ from AB towards AC.

slides.heading: Acceleration due to gravity from G, M and R
slides.body_md: A body of mass $m$ at the surface of a planet of mass $M$ and radius $R$ is pulled with $F = \dfrac{G M m}{R^2} = m g$.
bullets: g does not depend on the mass m of the falling body, so all bodies fall alike (air resistance apart).
For the Earth, $\dfrac{GM}{R^2} = \dfrac{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 6.0 \times 10^{24}}{(6.4 \times 10^6)^2} \approx 9.77$ m s$^{-2}$; we use $9.8$ m s$^{-2}$.
Weight of a body is mg: the pull of the planet on it. Mass is a property of the body; weight changes with g.
Larger radius at fixed density means larger g; the Moon, being smaller, has a smaller g.

rows: h much less than R for the approximation
Uniform density; only the inner sphere pulls

visual.alt: Table of the acceleration due to gravity at the surface, at a height, at a depth and at the centre of the Earth

slides.narration: At the surface the weight of a body is the gravitational pull, so g equals G M over R squared. It does not depend on the mass of the falling body. For the Earth it comes to about nine point eight metres per second squared. A planet of the same density but larger radius has a larger g, because g is four thirds pi G rho R.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: g on the Moon
slides.body_md: The Moon has $M = 7.35 \times 10^{22}$ kg and $R = 1.74 \times 10^6$ m. Find g on its surface and the weight of a $60$ kg astronaut there.
bullets: Weight $= m g_M = 60 \times 1.62 = 97.2$ N, about $\dfrac{1}{6}$ of her weight on the Earth.

rows: h much less than R for the approximation
Uniform density; only the inner sphere pulls

visual.alt: Table of the acceleration due to gravity at the surface, at a height, at a depth and at the centre of the Earth

slides.narration: Put the Moon’s mass and radius into G M over R squared. The answer is about 1.62 metres per second squared, roughly one sixth of the Earth’s value. A sixty kilogram astronaut therefore weighs about 97.2 newtons on the Moon, while her mass is still sixty kilograms.

slides.heading: g above the surface
slides.body_md: At height $h$ the distance from the centre is $R + h$, so $g' = \dfrac{G M}{(R+h)^2}$.
bullets: g′ decreases with height; at h = R it is g/4.
Binomial approximation $(1 + x)^{-2} \approx 1 - 2x$ is good only for small $x = h/R$.
Weight falls in the same proportion: a body weighs less at the top of a mountain.

slides.narration: Above the surface, the distance from the centre of the Earth is the radius plus the height, so g falls as the inverse square of that distance. At a height equal to the radius, g is a quarter of its surface value. For heights much smaller than the radius, the binomial theorem gives g prime approximately equal to g times one minus two h over R.

slides.heading: g below the surface
slides.body_md: Assume a uniform Earth of density $\rho$. A body at depth $d$ is at distance $r = R - d$ from the centre.
bullets: The shell above it pulls with zero net force on the body; only the **inner sphere** of radius r attracts it, as if its mass were at the centre.
Inner mass $= \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \rho$, so $g' = \dfrac{G \cdot \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \rho}{r^2} = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi G \rho\, r = g\,\dfrac{r}{R}$.
Hence $g' = g\left(1 - \dfrac{d}{R}\right)$: linear fall to **zero at the centre**.
Real Earth is denser near the centre, so the true g first rises slightly with depth; the uniform model is the textbook approximation.

visual.caption: g is zero at the centre, largest at the surface and falls as 1/r² outside.

slides.narration: Inside a uniform Earth, the shell of matter outside the body pulls with no net force. Only the inner sphere of radius r attracts it. Its mass is proportional to r cubed, so g prime is proportional to r. That gives g prime equals g times one minus d over R, falling in a straight line to zero at the centre. The graph shows this linear fall inside and the inverse square fall outside.

In this part we use energy to understand both: gravitational potential energy and potential, the escape speed, and the speed, period and energy of a satellite.

slides.heading: Gravitational potential energy
slides.body_md: Take the potential energy to be zero when the two masses are infinitely far apart. Bringing $m$ from infinity to distance $r$ from $M$, gravity does positive work, so the energy becomes **negative**:
bullets: As $m$ moves in from $x = \infty$ to $x = r$ gravity does work $W = \int_r^{\infty} \dfrac{G M m}{x^2}\,dx = \dfrac{G M m}{r}$, and $U(r) = U(\infty) - W = -\dfrac{G M m}{r}$.
Equivalently, an outside agent must supply $+\dfrac{G M m}{r}$ to take $m$ back to infinity.
U belongs to the **pair** of masses, increases (becomes less negative) as r increases, and tends to 0 at infinity.
The force is conservative: the work depends only on the end points, not the path.

x.label: distance from the centre, r / R

visual.alt: Graph of gravitational potential energy in units of GMm over R against distance in units of R: a curve starting at minus one at the surface and rising towards zero at large distance
visual.caption: U is negative everywhere and rises towards 0 as r increases.

slides.narration: We choose the potential energy to be zero when the masses are infinitely far apart. As the mass comes in from infinity, gravity does positive work, so the energy becomes negative, minus G M m over r. The graph rises towards zero as the distance grows. The energy belongs to the pair of masses, and because gravity is conservative the work between two points does not depend on the path.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a satellite’s potential energy
slides.body_md: A $250$ kg satellite is at a distance $r = 1.0 \times 10^7$ m from the centre of the Earth ($G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}$, $M_E = 6.0 \times 10^{24}$ kg). Find its gravitational potential energy and the gravitational potential there.
bullets: $U = -\dfrac{G M m}{r} = -\dfrac{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 6.0 \times 10^{24} \times 250}{1.0 \times 10^7} = -1.00 \times 10^{10}$ J.
$V = \dfrac{U}{m} = -\dfrac{G M}{r} = -4.00 \times 10^{7}$ J kg$^{-1}$.

slides.narration: The potential energy is minus G M m over r. With the stated numbers it comes to about minus 10.0 times ten to the power nine joules. Dividing by the mass of the satellite gives the gravitational potential, about minus 40.0 million joules per kilogram.

slides.heading: Gravitational potential
slides.body_md: The **gravitational potential** at a point is the potential energy per unit mass there: $V = \dfrac{U}{m}$.
bullets: V is the work done **per kilogram** by an outside agent in bringing a test mass slowly from infinity to the point, with a sign: V is negative.
Potential is a **scalar**: potentials of several masses add as plain numbers (unlike fields, which add as vectors).
Unit: joule per kilogram (J kg⁻¹). Potential energy of a mass m at that point: U = m V.
Potential energy of a system of masses: add −G m_i m_j / r_ij over every pair once.

rows: Gravitational potential energy of m at distance r

visual.alt: Table comparing gravitational potential energy and gravitational potential: symbol, unit and kind

slides.narration: The gravitational potential is the potential energy per unit mass. It equals minus G M over r, it is negative, and it is a scalar. That means the potential at a point due to several masses is found by adding ordinary numbers, with no vectors needed. The potential energy of a mass there is simply the mass times the potential.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: potential of two masses
slides.body_md: Masses of $5$ kg and $10$ kg are $0.5$ m apart. Find the gravitational potential at the point on the line between them, $0.2$ m from the lighter mass.
bullets: Distances: $0.2$ m from the $5$ kg mass and $0.5 - 0.2 = 0.3$ m from the $10$ kg mass.
Scalars add: no directions needed. (The gravitational field there is a vector and is found separately.)

slides.heading: Near the surface: why U = mgh works
slides.body_md: Raising $m$ from $R$ to $R + h$ changes the potential energy by $\Delta U = G M m\left(\dfrac{1}{R} - \dfrac{1}{R+h}\right) = \dfrac{G M m\, h}{R(R+h)}$.
bullets: Used $GM = gR^2$. For $h \ll R$ the denominator is about $R$, giving the familiar $mgh$.
For large h the exact result is smaller than m g h: g decreases as you rise, so g h overestimates the work.
The table shows how mgh drifts away from the exact value for heights up to R.

headers: g h is too big by

visual.alt: Table comparing the exact change of potential energy per kilogram with g h for heights from 1 kilometre to 6400 kilometres

math: \Delta U = \dfrac{m g R\, h}{R + h} \;\approx\; m g h \quad (h \ll R)
slides.narration: The exact change of potential energy between the surface and a height h is m g R h divided by R plus h. When h is much smaller than R this is just m g h. The table shows that the simple formula is accurate to about a hundredth of a percent for a one kilometre climb, but overestimates by about nine percent at six hundred and forty kilometres, and by fifty percent at a height equal to the radius.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: lifting a package to 3200 km
slides.body_md: How much work must be done to raise a $120$ kg package from the Earth’s surface to a height of $3200$ km? Take $g = 9.8$ m s$^{-2}$, $R = 6.4 \times 10^6$ m. Compare with $mgh$.
bullets: $W = \Delta U = \dfrac{m g R h}{R + h} = \dfrac{120 \times 9.8 \times 6.4 \times 10^6 \times 3.2 \times 10^6}{9.6 \times 10^6} = 2.51 \times 10^{9}$ J.
The naive value $m g h = 120 \times 9.8 \times 3.2 \times 10^6 = 3.76 \times 10^{9}$ J is too large by 50.0% of the true work.

headers: g h is too big by

slides.narration: Use the exact formula, because the height is not small compared with the radius. It gives 2.509 times ten to the power nine joules. The simple formula m g h would give 3.763 times ten to the power nine joules, which is fifty percent too large.

slides.heading: Escape speed
slides.body_md: The **escape speed** is the minimum speed that lets a body leave the planet and never return (air resistance ignored). It needs total energy $\ge 0$.
bullets: Earth: $v_e = \sqrt{2 \times 9.8 \times 6.4 \times 10^6} = 11.2$ km s$^{-1}$.
It does not depend on the mass of the body, nor on the direction of launch (if nothing obstructs it).
It is √2 times the orbital speed near the surface.
A body launched at v < v_e rises to a finite height and falls back.

visual.alt: Table of the mass, radius and escape speed of the Earth, the Moon and Mars computed from root of 2GM over R

math: \tfrac{1}{2} m v_e^2 - \dfrac{G M m}{R} = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; v_e = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 G M}{R}} = \sqrt{2 g R}
slides.narration: To escape, a body must reach infinity with at least zero speed. Setting the total energy to zero gives the escape speed, the square root of two G M over R, which is also the square root of two g R. For the Earth it comes to eleven point two kilometres per second. It does not depend on the mass of the body or on the direction in which it is launched.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: leaving Mars
slides.body_md: Mars has $M = 6.4 \times 10^{23}$ kg and $R = 3.4 \times 10^6$ m. Find the escape speed.
bullets: $v_e = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 G M}{R}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 \times 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 6.4 \times 10^{23}}{3.4 \times 10^6}} = \sqrt{2.51 \times 10^{7}}$ m s$^{-1}$
$= 5011$ m s$^{-1}$ $= 5.01$ km s$^{-1}$, less than half the Earth’s value.

slides.narration: Put the mass and radius of Mars into root two G M over R. The speed is about 5.01 kilometres per second, less than half the escape speed from the Earth, because Mars is much less massive.

slides.heading: Orbital speed and period
slides.body_md: A satellite in a circular orbit of radius $r = R + h$ is kept moving in a circle by gravity alone:
bullets: Near the surface ($r \approx R$): $v = \sqrt{gR} = 7.92$ km s$^{-1}$ and $T = 2\pi\sqrt{R/g} \approx 84.6$ minutes.
v and T depend only on the orbit radius and the central mass, **not on the satellite’s mass**.
A higher orbit is slower and has a longer period (Kepler’s law of periods again).
Newton’s cannon: below v the body falls, at v it circles, between v and √2 v it follows an ellipse, at √2 v it escapes.

visual.alt: Newton cannon: launches at less than, equal to, a little more than and root two times the circular speed give a fall back, a circle, an ellipse and an escape
visual.caption: Faster launches go farther; at root two times the circular speed the body escapes.

math: \dfrac{m v^2}{r} = \dfrac{G M m}{r^2} \;\Rightarrow\; v = \sqrt{\dfrac{G M}{r}}, \qquad T = \dfrac{2\pi r}{v} = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{r^3}{G M}}
slides.narration: A satellite is in free fall all the time: gravity supplies exactly the force needed for circular motion. Equating the two gives the orbital speed, root G M over r, and the period, two pi root r cubed over G M. Neither depends on the mass of the satellite. Near the Earth’s surface the speed is about seven point nine kilometres per second and the period about eighty five minutes.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: a satellite at one Earth radius above the surface
slides.body_md: A satellite orbits at a height $h = R$ above the Earth. Take $g = 9.8$ m s$^{-2}$ and $R = 6.4 \times 10^6$ m. Find its speed and period.
bullets: $T = \dfrac{2\pi r}{v} = \dfrac{2\pi \times 1.28 \times 10^{7}}{5600} = 14360$ s $\approx 3.99$ h.

slides.heading: Higher orbit, lower speed, easier escape
slides.body_md: Orbital speed and escape speed against orbit radius:
bullets: Both fall as 1/√r; the escape speed is always √2 times the orbital speed at the same radius.
To go from a lower to a higher circular orbit a satellite loses speed, even though it must be given energy.
In the lowest orbits air drag removes energy and the satellite spirals in, speeding up.

visual.alt: Graph of orbital speed and escape speed in kilometres per second against distance from the Earth centre: both fall with distance and the escape curve is root two times higher
visual.caption: Higher orbits are slower; escape speed is always √2 times the orbital speed at the same r.

slides.narration: Both curves fall with distance, and the escape curve always lies root two times above the orbital curve. This explains a surprising fact: moving to a higher circular orbit means the satellite ends up moving more slowly, even though we had to supply energy to raise it. If air drag removes energy in a low orbit, the satellite sinks to a lower orbit and speeds up.

slides.heading: Energy of an orbiting satellite
slides.body_md: In a circular orbit of radius $r$, with $v^2 = \dfrac{G M}{r}$:
bullets: The total energy is **negative**: the satellite is bound. The magnitude |E| = K is the **binding energy**, the extra energy that would free it.
U = −2K, so E = U/2.
To raise the orbit radius from r₁ to r₂, the energy needed is ΔE = (G M m / 2)(1/r₁ − 1/r₂).
Losing energy to drag makes E more negative: r decreases and K increases.

visual.alt: Graph of kinetic, potential and total energy of a satellite in a circular orbit against orbit radius: kinetic energy positive and falling, potential energy negative and twice as large in magnitude as the total, total energy negative and equal to minus the kinetic energy
visual.caption: E = −K = U/2 at every orbit radius.

math: K = \tfrac{1}{2} m v^2 = \dfrac{G M m}{2r}, \quad U = -\dfrac{G M m}{r}, \quad E = K + U = -\dfrac{G M m}{2r} = -K
slides.narration: In a circular orbit the kinetic energy is G M m over two r, the potential energy is minus G M m over r, and the total energy is minus G M m over two r, equal to minus the kinetic energy. The total is negative because the satellite is bound. The kinetic energy is the binding energy: that much extra energy would free the satellite. Raising the orbit needs energy, but the satellite slows down.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: raising an orbit
slides.body_md: A $400$ kg satellite is moved from a circular orbit of radius $8.0 \times 10^6$ m to one of radius $1.2 \times 10^7$ m. Find its total energy in each orbit and the energy needed ($G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}$, $M_E = 6.0 \times 10^{24}$ kg).
bullets: The speed falls from the lower orbit to the higher one, so the energy goes into potential energy.

visual.alt: Graph of kinetic, potential and total energy of a satellite in a circular orbit against orbit radius: kinetic energy positive and falling, potential energy negative and twice as large in magnitude as the total, total energy negative and equal to minus the kinetic energy
visual.caption: E = −K = U/2 at every orbit radius.

slides.narration: The energy in the lower orbit is minus 10.01 times ten to the power nine joules and in the higher orbit minus 6.670 times ten to the power nine joules. The difference, 3.335 times ten to the power nine joules, is the energy that must be supplied.

slides.narration: To sum up. The potential energy of two masses is minus G M m over r and the potential is minus G M over r. The escape speed is root two G M over R, which is eleven point two kilometres per second for the Earth. A satellite in a circular orbit has speed root G M over r, a period two pi root r cubed over G M, and a total energy equal to minus its kinetic energy.

slides.heading: Exam tips — Part 2
bullets: Say where U = 0 (at infinity) before using −GMm/r; check that signs give a negative U and negative E for bound orbits.
Use g R² in place of G M when the problem gives g and R, and say so.
Derive v_e from energy conservation and v_orbit from F = mv²/r; do not mix them up.
Use the exact ΔU = mgRh/(R+h) when h is not much smaller than R; ΔU = mgh only for small h.

slides.narration: Always say that the potential energy is taken as zero at infinity, and check that your signs make bound energies negative. Use g R squared for G M when the data are given that way. Derive the escape speed from energy and the orbital speed from the force. And use m g h only when the height is small compared with the radius.

sections.heading: 1. Kepler’s laws, the law of gravitation and superposition
sections.body_md:
- **Kepler’s laws:** (1) each planet moves in an ellipse with the Sun at one focus; (2) the line from the Sun to the planet sweeps equal areas in equal times (angular momentum is conserved because gravity is central, so a planet is fastest at perihelion: $v_p r_p = v_a r_a$); (3) $T^2 \propto a^3$ with $a$ the semi-major axis. For a circular orbit $T^2 = \dfrac{4\pi^2}{GM}r^3$. A body at $2.25$ AU has $T = 3.375$ years.
- **Newton’s law:** $F = \dfrac{G m_1 m_2}{r^2}$, attractive, along the line joining the bodies, equal and opposite on the two; $G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}$ N m² kg⁻². The Sun pulls the Earth with $3.56 \times 10^{22}$ N ($M_S = 2.0 \times 10^{30}$ kg, $r = 1.5 \times 10^{11}$ m).
- **Superposition:** the force on a body from several masses is the vector sum of the individual pulls. A 4.0 kg mass with 2.0 kg at 0.30 m and 3.0 kg at 0.40 m (perpendicular) feels $7.76$ nN at $40.2^\circ$ from the line to the 2.0 kg mass.
- A uniform sphere acts on outside bodies as if its whole mass were at its centre.

Half the longest diameter of the ellipse; the length that enters T² ∝ a³.
The net gravitational force is the vector sum of the forces due to the individual masses.

sections.heading: 2. Acceleration due to gravity and its variation
sections.body_md:
- **At the surface:** $g = \dfrac{GM}{R^2} = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi G\rho R$; independent of the mass of the falling body. On the Moon $g = 1.62$ m s⁻², about one sixth of the Earth’s.
- **Above the surface:** $g' = g\left(\dfrac{R}{R+h}\right)^2 \approx g\left(1 - \dfrac{2h}{R}\right)$ for $h \ll R$. At $h = R$, $g' = g/4$. At 320 km the exact value is $8.889$ m s⁻² against $8.820$ from the approximation.
- **Below the surface** (uniform Earth): only the inner sphere attracts, so $g' = g\left(1 - \dfrac{d}{R}\right)$, falling linearly to zero at the centre; at 320 km deep $g' = 9.310$ m s⁻². Over the same small distance, g falls twice as fast above the surface (2h/R) as below it (d/R).
- Weight $mg$ varies with place while mass does not; the Earth’s rotation and its non-uniform density are not considered here.

At depth d only the mass within radius R − d attracts a body; the shell above exerts no net force.

sections.heading: 3. Gravitational potential energy and potential
sections.body_md:
- With zero at infinity, $U(r) = -\dfrac{GMm}{r}$: negative, rising towards zero as $r$ increases. A $250$ kg satellite at $1.0 \times 10^7$ m has $U = -1.00 \times 10^{10}$ J.
- **Potential** $V = U/m = -\dfrac{GM}{r}$ is a scalar, so potentials of several masses add as numbers; $U = mV$. Two masses (5.0 kg and 10 kg) 0.50 m apart give $V = -3.89 \times 10^{-9}$ J kg⁻¹ at 0.20 m from the lighter one.
- Gravity is conservative: the work between two points depends only on the end points.
- **Near the surface:** $\Delta U = \dfrac{mgRh}{R+h} \approx mgh$ for $h \ll R$; the exact value is smaller than $mgh$ because g decreases with height. Lifting 120 kg through 3200 km needs $2.51 \times 10^{9}$ J, not $3.76 \times 10^{9}$ J.

sections.heading: 4. Escape speed, orbital speed and energy of a satellite
sections.body_md:
- **Escape speed:** $\tfrac{1}{2}mv_e^2 - \dfrac{GMm}{R} = 0$ gives $v_e = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}} = \sqrt{2gR}$: 11.2 km s⁻¹ for the Earth, 2.37 km s⁻¹ for the Moon, 5.01 km s⁻¹ for Mars. It does not depend on the projectile’s mass or the direction of launch.
- **Circular orbit:** $\dfrac{mv^2}{r} = \dfrac{GMm}{r^2}$ gives $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{r}}$ and $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{r^3}{GM}}$, independent of the satellite’s mass; $v_e = \sqrt{2}\,v$. Close to the Earth $v = \sqrt{gR} \approx 7.9$ km s⁻¹ and $T \approx 85$ minutes. At $h = R$: $v = 5.60$ km s⁻¹, $T \approx 3.99$ h.
- **Energy:** $K = \dfrac{GMm}{2r}$, $U = -\dfrac{GMm}{r}$, $E = -\dfrac{GMm}{2r} = -K$. Negative E means the satellite is bound; $|E|$ is the binding energy. Raising a 400 kg satellite from $8.0 \times 10^6$ m to $1.2 \times 10^7$ m needs $3.33 \times 10^{9}$ J although its speed decreases.
- Air drag lowers E, so the orbit shrinks and the speed rises.
- Geostationary and polar satellites and weightlessness are not treated in this chapter (see the README for the scope decision).

cards.front_md: State Kepler’s law of orbits.
cards.back_md: Each planet moves in an ellipse with the Sun at one focus.

cards.front_md: State Kepler’s law of areas.
cards.back_md: The line from the Sun to a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal intervals of time.

cards.front_md: State Kepler’s law of periods.
cards.back_md: The square of the period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis: $T^2 \propto a^3$.

cards.front_md: Why is a planet fastest at perihelion?
cards.back_md: Gravity is central, so angular momentum is conserved: $v r$ is constant at the extreme points, and r is smallest at perihelion.

cards.front_md: Write Newton’s law of gravitation.
cards.back_md: $F = G m_1 m_2/r^2$, attractive and along the line joining the bodies.

cards.front_md: Value and unit of G.
If the distance between two masses is doubled, what happens to the force?
cards.back_md: It falls to one quarter (inverse-square law).

cards.front_md: How do you find the force on a mass due to several others?
cards.back_md: Add the individual forces as vectors (superposition).

cards.front_md: Orbit period of a body at 9.0 AU from the Sun?
Write g in terms of G, M and R.
Does g depend on the mass of the falling body?
cards.back_md: No: the mass cancels in $a = F/m = GM/R^2$.

cards.front_md: Write g at a height h above the surface.
cards.back_md: $g' = g R^2/(R+h)^2 \approx g(1 - 2h/R)$ for $h \ll R$.

cards.front_md: What is g at a height equal to the Earth’s radius?
Write g at a depth d (uniform Earth).
What is g at the centre of the Earth (uniform model)?
cards.back_md: Zero.

cards.front_md: Why does only the inner sphere pull a body at depth d?
cards.back_md: The shell outside radius R − d exerts zero net force on a body inside it.

cards.front_md: Which falls faster over a small distance x: g above or below the surface?
cards.back_md: Above: the fractional fall is 2x/R against x/R below.

cards.front_md: Same density, radius doubled: what happens to g?
cards.back_md: It doubles, since $g = \tfrac{4}{3}\pi G\rho R$.

cards.front_md: Write the gravitational potential energy of m at distance r from M.
cards.back_md: $U = -GMm/r$ (zero at infinity).

cards.front_md: Why is U negative?
cards.back_md: Gravity does positive work as the mass comes in from infinity, where U = 0.

cards.front_md: Define gravitational potential.
cards.back_md: Potential energy per unit mass: $V = -GM/r$, a scalar; unit J kg⁻¹.

cards.front_md: How do potentials of several masses combine?
cards.back_md: Add them as scalars.

cards.front_md: Exact work to raise m from R to R + h?
cards.back_md: $mgRh/(R+h)$, which tends to $mgh$ for small h.

cards.front_md: Write the escape speed.
cards.back_md: $v_e = \sqrt{2GM/R} = \sqrt{2gR}$; 11.2 km/s for the Earth.

cards.front_md: Does escape speed depend on the projectile’s mass?
cards.back_md: No; the mass cancels from the energy condition.

cards.front_md: Orbital speed of a satellite at radius r?
cards.back_md: $v = \sqrt{GM/r}$, independent of the satellite’s mass.

cards.front_md: Period of a circular orbit?
cards.back_md: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{r^3/GM}$.

cards.front_md: Ratio of escape speed to orbital speed at the same radius?
Write K, U and E for a satellite in a circular orbit.
cards.back_md: $K = GMm/2r$, $U = -GMm/r$, $E = -GMm/2r = -K$.

cards.front_md: Exam tip: what happens to a low satellite as air drag removes energy?
cards.back_md: E becomes more negative, so r decreases and the speed increases.

questions.stem_md: A periodic comet moves round the Sun in a long elliptical orbit with the Sun at one focus. The comet has its greatest speed when it is

options.text_md: farthest from the Sun, where the Sun’s pull on it is weakest
at the ends of the minor axis, where the pull is perpendicular to its path
at every point equally, because the force always points to the Sun
nearest the Sun, because the line joining it to the Sun must sweep equal areas in equal times

questions.solution_md: Equal areas in equal times means a short radius needs a long arc in the same time, so the speed is greatest at perihelion — option (d).

9.0 years

27 years

questions.solution_md: $T^2 \propto a^3$, so $T^2 = 9.0^3 = 729$ and $T = \sqrt{729} = 27$ years — option (d).

19.6 N, directed towards the book

questions.solution_md: Gravitational forces between two bodies are an equal and opposite pair (Newton’s third law), so the book pulls the Earth with the same magnitude, towards the book — option (d).

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A: with the smaller a, Mercury has the smaller T — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A small body placed exactly midway between two identical masses, far from everything else, feels no net gravitational force from them.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. The two pulls are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, so their vector sum is zero (superposition).

questions.stem_md: True or false? When the distance between two planets is doubled, the gravitational attraction between them is reduced to half its value.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. The force varies as 1/r², so doubling the distance reduces it to **one quarter**.

questions.stem_md: Two oil tankers, each of mass 2.0 × 10⁸ kg, float with their centres 100 m apart. Take G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². Find the gravitational force between them, in N.

marking_scheme.step: F = G m₁m₂/r² with the given values

questions.stem_md: Three identical spheres of mass 30 kg sit at the corners of an equilateral triangle of side 0.60 m, in free space. With G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², find the magnitude of the net gravitational force on one sphere, in units of 10⁻⁷ N.
questions.solution_md: Each of the other two spheres pulls with $F_1 = \dfrac{G m^2}{a^2} = 1.668 \times 10^{-7}$ N, along the sides at $60^\circ$ to each other. The components perpendicular to the bisector cancel, so $F = 2F_1\cos 30^\circ = \sqrt{3}\,F_1 = 1.732 \times 1.668 \times 10^{-7} = 2.888 \times 10^{-7}$ N. In units of $10^{-7}$ N: $F = 2.89$.

questions.stem_md: Two bodies of mass 16 kg and 9 kg are 7.0 m apart, far from all other matter. A small test mass lies on the line joining them. How far from the 16 kg body must it be for the net gravitational force on it to be zero, in m?
questions.solution_md: At the point of zero force the pulls are equal: $\dfrac{G m \times 16}{x^2} = \dfrac{G m \times 9}{(7.0 - x)^2}$. Taking square roots, $\dfrac{x}{7.0 - x} = \sqrt{\dfrac{16}{9}} = \dfrac{4}{3}$, so $3x = 4(7.0 - x)$, $7x = 28$ and $x = 4$ m.

marking_scheme.step: x = 4 m from the 16 kg body

questions.stem_md: A periodic comet takes 64 years to go once round the Sun, and at perihelion it is 0.40 AU from the Sun. Using Earth’s period (1 year at 1 AU), find its greatest distance from the Sun, in AU.
questions.solution_md: $a^3 = T^2 = 64^2 = 4096$ in AU³ and year², so the semi-major axis is $a = \sqrt[3]{4096} = 16.0$ AU. The ellipse has perihelion plus aphelion $= 2a$, so $r_a = 2a - r_p = 2 \times 16.0 - 0.40 = 31.6$ AU.

questions.stem_md: The Earth is 1.47 × 10¹¹ m from the Sun at perihelion, where its orbital speed is 30.3 km/s, and 1.52 × 10¹¹ m away at aphelion. Find its speed at aphelion, in km/s.
questions.solution_md: At perihelion and aphelion the velocity is perpendicular to the radius, so angular momentum conservation gives $v_a r_a = v_p r_p$ and $v_a = v_p\,\dfrac{r_p}{r_a} = 30.3 \times \dfrac{1.47}{1.52} = 29.3$ km/s.

questions.stem_md: Match each statement about the planets in List I with the law or principle in List II that explains it.

options.text_md: Mercury moves fastest when it is nearest the Sun
The Sun is not at the centre of a planet’s path but at one focus of it
A planet four times as far from the Sun as another takes eight times as long to go round
When the distance from the Sun is doubled, the Sun’s pull on a planet falls to a quarter

questions.solution_md: Faster near the Sun: areas (q). Sun at a focus: orbits (s). Period 8 times for a 4 times radius, since 4^1.5 = 8: periods (p). Quarter pull at twice the distance: inverse-square law (r).

questions.stem_md: Use the idea of angular momentum to explain why a planet moves faster when it is closer to the Sun.

answer.model_answer_md: The Sun’s pull on the planet acts along the line joining them, so its torque about the Sun is zero and the planet’s angular momentum about the Sun is constant. At the nearest and farthest points $L = m v r$, so $v r$ is constant: a smaller $r$ means a larger speed $v$.

questions.solution_md: Torque zero, L constant, v r constant.

marking_scheme.step: Gravity is central: zero torque, angular momentum conserved
L = m v r constant, so smaller r means larger v

questions.stem_md: A 0.20 kg apple falls from a branch. Explain, with numbers, why the apple’s pull on the Earth makes no noticeable difference to the Earth’s motion.

answer.model_answer_md: The Earth pulls the apple with $F = mg = 1.96$ N, so by the third law the apple pulls the Earth with the same $1.96$ N. The Earth’s acceleration is $F/M = 1.96 / (6.0 \times 10^{24}) = 3.27 \times 10^{-25}$ m s$^{-2}$, far too small to detect.

questions.solution_md: Equal forces; a = F/M is negligible for the huge mass of the Earth.

marking_scheme.step: Equal and opposite forces of 1.96 N
a = F/M = 3.27 × 10⁻²⁵ m s⁻²: negligible because M is huge

questions.stem_md: Two students of mass 60 kg each stand 1.0 m apart. Treating them as point masses, find the gravitational force between them (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²) and compare it with the weight of a 0.10 g paper clip. Why do we not notice such forces?

answer.model_answer_md: $F = \dfrac{G m^2}{r^2} = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 3600 / 1.0 = 2.40 \times 10^{-7}$ N. The weight of the clip is $0.10 \times 10^{-3} \times 9.8 = 9.80 \times 10^{-4}$ N, about 4100 times larger. G is so small that gravity is noticeable only when at least one body is as massive as a planet; the forces between everyday objects are swamped by other forces such as friction.

questions.solution_md: F ≈ 2.4 × 10⁻⁷ N; the clip’s weight is about 4100 times larger.

marking_scheme.step: Clip’s weight 9.80 × 10⁻⁴ N, about 4100 times larger
G is tiny; the effect is swamped by other forces

questions.stem_md: State Newton’s universal law of gravitation, write it in symbols and give two properties of the gravitational force between two point masses.

answer.model_answer_md: Every particle in the universe attracts every other with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them: $F = G m_1 m_2 / r^2$, where $G$ is the universal constant. The force is always attractive, acts along the line joining the particles, and forms an equal and opposite pair on the two bodies.

questions.solution_md: Statement, formula, two properties.

marking_scheme.step: Two properties (attractive, along the line, mutual/equal and opposite)

questions.stem_md: A planet of mass m moves in a circular orbit of radius r about a star of mass M. Derive the relation between its period T and r, and say what law of Kepler this gives.

answer.model_answer_md: A planet in a circular orbit is held there by gravity alone, so the gravitational force supplies the centripetal force: $\dfrac{GMm}{r^2} = m\omega^2 r$ with $\omega = 2\pi/T$. Cancelling $m$ and rearranging gives $T^2 = \dfrac{4\pi^2}{GM}\,r^3$. For one star the factor $4\pi^2/GM$ is the same for every planet, so $T^2$ is proportional to $r^3$. This is Kepler’s law of periods, here for a circular orbit.

questions.solution_md: Force equals m ω² r; T² = 4π² r³/(GM).

questions.stem_md: Mars has mass 6.4 × 10²³ kg and radius 3.4 × 10⁶ m. Using G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², find the acceleration due to gravity at its surface, in m/s².
Take g = 9.8 m/s² at the Earth’s surface and R = 6.4 × 10⁶ m. Find the acceleration due to gravity at a height of 3200 km above the surface, in m/s².
questions.solution_md: $g' = g\left(\dfrac{R}{R+h}\right)^2 = 9.8 \times \left(\dfrac{6.4 \times 10^6}{9.6 \times 10^6}\right)^2 = 9.8 \times 0.4444 = 4.36$ m/s².

marking_scheme.step: g′ = g R²/(R + h)² with R + h = 9.6 × 10⁶ m

questions.stem_md: A Himalayan summit is 8.8 km above sea level. Using the small-height approximation and R = 6.4 × 10⁶ m, find by what percentage g is smaller there than at sea level.
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{\Delta g}{g} \approx \dfrac{2h}{R} = \dfrac{2 \times 8.8 \times 10^3}{6.4 \times 10^6} = 0.00275$, so $\dfrac{\Delta g}{g} \times 100 = 0.275$ per cent. (The exact formula gives 0.274 per cent.)

questions.stem_md: Assume the Earth is a uniform sphere with g = 9.8 m/s² at the surface and R = 6.4 × 10⁶ m. A borehole reaches a depth of 1600 km. Find g at the bottom, in m/s².
questions.solution_md: $g' = g\left(1 - \dfrac{d}{R}\right) = 9.8 \times \left(1 - \dfrac{1.6 \times 10^6}{6.4 \times 10^6}\right) = 9.8 \times 0.75 = 7.35$ m/s².

questions.stem_md: A 60 kg astronaut is at a height of 400 km above the Earth’s surface. Taking g = 9.8 m/s² and R = 6.4 × 10⁶ m, find the gravitational force of the Earth on her, in N.
questions.solution_md: $g' = 9.8 \times \left(\dfrac{6.4}{6.8}\right)^2 = 8.681$ m/s², so $F = m g' = 60 \times 8.681 = 521$ N, about 89% of her weight on the ground ($588$ N).

questions.stem_md: An exoplanet has 0.10 times the mass and 0.50 times the radius of the Earth. If g at the Earth’s surface is 9.8 m/s², g at its surface is

options.text_md: 4.9 m/s²
9.8 m/s²

questions.stem_md: At what height above the Earth’s surface is the acceleration due to gravity one quarter of its value at the surface? (R is the radius of the Earth.)

options.text_md: 2R
R
4R

questions.solution_md: g′ = g R²/(R + h)² = g/4 needs (R + h)² = 4R², so R + h = 2R and h = R — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Inside a uniform spherical Earth of radius R, at what depth below the surface is g equal to half its surface value?

options.text_md: R

questions.solution_md: g′ = g(1 − d/R) = g/2 gives d = R/2 — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A tower of height x and a mine shaft of depth x are both very small compared with the Earth’s radius R. Compared with the value at the surface, the fractional decrease in g at the top of the tower is

options.text_md: twice the fractional decrease at the bottom of the shaft, 2x/R against x/R
half the fractional decrease at the bottom of the shaft
equal to the fractional decrease at the bottom of the shaft
zero, because the Earth’s mass is unchanged

questions.solution_md: Above the surface g falls by the fraction 2x/R; below it (uniform Earth) by x/R, so the tower’s decrease is twice as large — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Two planets have the same mean density, and their radii are in the ratio 1 : 2. The ratio of the accelerations due to gravity at their surfaces is
questions.solution_md: g = (4/3)πGρR, so at equal density g ∝ R and the ratio is 1 : 2 — option (b).

questions.stem_md: In the model of a uniform Earth, a tunnel through the exact centre has g equal to ___ at the centre.
questions.solution_md: At the centre the inner sphere has zero radius, so g′ = g(1 − R/R) = **zero**.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Inside a uniform spherical Earth, g decreases in direct proportion to the distance moved from the surface towards the centre.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. g′ = g(1 − d/R) falls linearly with the depth d, reaching zero at the centre.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** At the bottom of a mine 3.2 km deep, g is slightly less than at the surface.

**Reason (R):** The formula g = GM/r², with M the whole mass of the Earth, holds at every depth.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: g′ = g(1 − d/R). R is false: below the surface only the mass inside radius r attracts, so M must be replaced by the inner mass — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** At a height equal to the Earth’s radius above the surface, g is half its surface value.

**Reason (R):** Above the surface, g varies inversely as the square of the distance from the centre of the Earth.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: R is true, but at h = R the distance is 2R so g falls to g/4, not g/2: A is false — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The Earth pulls a heavier stone with a greater force than a lighter one. Why, then, do both fall with the same acceleration near the surface?

answer.model_answer_md: The force on a stone of mass $m$ is $G M m/R^2$, but its acceleration is force divided by mass: $a = GM/R^2 = g$. The mass $m$ cancels, because the greater pull on the heavier stone is exactly offset by its greater inertia.

questions.solution_md: a = F/m = GM/R²; m cancels.

marking_scheme.step: F = GMm/R² is proportional to m
a = F/m = GM/R²: independent of m (greater pull, greater inertia)

questions.stem_md: A miner reaches the centre of a uniform Earth. State, with a reason, what happens to her mass and to her weight there.

answer.model_answer_md: Her mass is unchanged: it is a property of the body. Her weight, the gravitational pull on her, becomes zero, because at the centre $g' = g(1 - d/R) = 0$ with $d = R$; equivalently, the Earth’s matter pulls equally in all directions and the pulls cancel.

questions.solution_md: Mass same; weight zero since g′ = 0.

marking_scheme.step: Weight zero: g′ = g(1 − R/R) = 0 (pulls cancel)

questions.stem_md: Derive the expression for the acceleration due to gravity at a height h above the Earth’s surface, and show that for h much smaller than R it is approximately g(1 − 2h/R).

answer.model_answer_md: Near the surface the pull on a body, per unit mass, is $GM/R^2 = g$. At a height $h$ the body is farther from the centre, at distance $R + h$, so the acceleration there is $g' = GM/(R+h)^2$, which can be written $g' = g(1 + h/R)^{-2}$. When $h$ is very small compared with $R$ we expand this with the binomial theorem and keep the first two terms, so $g' \approx g(1 - 2h/R)$.

questions.solution_md: g′ = GM/(R + h)² = g(1 + h/R)⁻²; expand.

marking_scheme.step: g = GM/R² and g′ = GM/(R + h)²

questions.stem_md: Taking the Earth to be a sphere of uniform density, derive the acceleration due to gravity at a depth d below the surface.

answer.model_answer_md: At depth $d$ the body is at distance $r = R - d$ from the centre. The shell of matter outside radius $r$ exerts no net force on it, so only the inner sphere attracts it. For uniform density the mass of that sphere is $M r^3/R^3$, so $g' = G M r^3/(R^3 r^2) = GMr/R^3 = g\,r/R$. Therefore $g' = g(1 - d/R)$, which falls linearly with depth and vanishes at the centre.

questions.solution_md: Inner mass Mr³/R³; g′ = g r/R.

marking_scheme.step: Only the inner sphere of radius R − d attracts

questions.stem_md: A satellite of mass m circles the Earth in an orbit of radius 2R, where R is the Earth’s radius and g is the surface value. With the zero of potential energy at infinite separation, its gravitational potential energy is

options.text_md: −mgR/2
+mgR/2
−mgR
−2mgR

questions.solution_md: U = −GMm/r with r = 2R and GM = gR²: U = −m g R²/(2R) = −mgR/2 — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A space probe is carried radially outwards from a planet, from distance r to a larger distance r′. Taking the potential energy as zero at infinity, the gravitational potential energy of the probe–planet system

options.text_md: decreases, because the pull on the probe weakens
stays the same, because the masses are unchanged
increases, becoming less negative, because work must be done against the pull
becomes positive as soon as the probe leaves the surface

questions.solution_md: U = −GMm/r rises towards zero as r grows; an outside agent has to supply the work — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A student uses mgh for the work done in lifting a satellite from the ground to a height h. This is accurate only when

options.text_md: the mass of the satellite is much smaller than the mass of the Earth
h is measured from the centre of the Earth
h is much smaller than the radius of the Earth, so that g stays nearly constant
the satellite is lifted at constant velocity

questions.solution_md: The exact change is mgRh/(R + h), which reduces to mgh when R + h ≈ R, that is h ≪ R — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Taking the potential energy to be zero at infinity, find the gravitational potential energy of a 2.0 kg object on the surface of the Earth, in units of 10⁸ J. Use G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², M = 6.0 × 10²⁴ kg and R = 6.4 × 10⁶ m. Give the sign.
questions.solution_md: $U = -\dfrac{G M m}{R} = -\dfrac{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 6.0 \times 10^{24} \times 2.0}{6.4 \times 10^6} = -1.25 \times 10^{8}$ J. In units of $10^8$ J: $U = -1.25$.

questions.stem_md: An agency lifts a 1500 kg satellite from the Earth’s surface to a height of 1600 km, where it is released. Take g = 9.8 m/s² and R = 6.4 × 10⁶ m. Find the minimum work done against gravity, in GJ (1 GJ = 10⁹ J).
questions.solution_md: $W = \Delta U = \dfrac{m g R h}{R + h} = \dfrac{1500 \times 9.8 \times 6.4 \times 10^6 \times 1.6 \times 10^6}{8.0 \times 10^6} = 1.88 \times 10^{10}$ J $= 18.8$ GJ. (The simple $mgh$ would give 23.5 GJ, which is too large because $g$ decreases with height.)

marking_scheme.step: ΔU = mgRh/(R + h) (exact, since h is not ≪ R)

questions.stem_md: Two identical spheres of mass 4.0 kg have their centres 1.0 m apart in free space. Find the gravitational potential at the midpoint of the line joining them, in units of 10⁻⁹ J/kg (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²). Give the sign.
questions.solution_md: Each sphere is 0.50 m from the midpoint, and potentials add as scalars: $V = -2\,\dfrac{G m}{0.50} = -2 \times \dfrac{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 4.0}{0.50} = -1.07 \times 10^{-9}$ J/kg. In units of $10^{-9}$ J/kg: $V = -1.07$. (The gravitational field there is zero, but the potential is not.)

marking_scheme.step: V = −Gm/0.50 for each sphere, added as scalars

questions.stem_md: Three identical 10 kg spheres are placed at the corners of an equilateral triangle of side 0.50 m. With the potential energy zero when they are infinitely far apart, find the gravitational potential energy of the system, in units of 10⁻⁸ J (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²).
questions.solution_md: There are three pairs, each at 0.50 m: $U = -3\,\dfrac{G m^2}{a} = -3 \times \dfrac{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 100}{0.50} = -4.00 \times 10^{-8}$ J. In units of $10^{-8}$ J: $U = -4.00$.

questions.stem_md: A meteoroid, at rest relative to the Earth at a height equal to the Earth’s radius above the surface, falls straight down. Neglecting air drag and the Earth’s rotation, with g = 9.8 m/s² and R = 6.4 × 10⁶ m, find its speed on reaching the surface, in km/s.
questions.solution_md: Energy conservation between $r = 2R$ and $r = R$: $\tfrac{1}{2}v^2 = GM\left(\dfrac{1}{R} - \dfrac{1}{2R}\right) = \dfrac{GM}{2R} = \dfrac{gR}{2}$, so $v = \sqrt{gR} = \sqrt{9.8 \times 6.4 \times 10^6} = 7920$ m/s $= 7.92$ km/s.

questions.stem_md: A probe is raised from the Earth’s surface to a height of 1280 km. By what percentage is the exact increase in its gravitational potential energy smaller than the value mgh? Take R = 6.4 × 10⁶ m, and give the percentage of mgh.
questions.solution_md: Exact $\Delta U = \dfrac{m g R h}{R + h}$, so $\dfrac{\Delta U}{mgh} = \dfrac{R}{R + h} = \dfrac{6.4 \times 10^6}{7.68 \times 10^6} = 0.8333$. The exact value is smaller than $mgh$ by the fraction $1 - 0.8333 = 0.1667$ of $mgh$, so in per cent of $mgh$: $\left(1 - 0.8333\right) \times 100 = 16.7$.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The gravitational potential energy of the Earth and a satellite orbiting it is negative.

**Reason (R):** The zero of potential energy is taken at infinite separation, and gravity does positive work as the satellite comes in from infinity.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true, and R explains A: U(∞) = 0 and U falls as the satellite is brought in — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? With the zero of potential energy at infinite separation, two masses at a finite separation have positive gravitational potential energy, because the force between them is attractive.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. Attraction means gravity does positive work as the masses come together from infinity, so U is **negative**: U = −Gm₁m₂/r.

questions.stem_md: Define the gravitational potential at a point and give its SI unit. How does it differ from the gravitational potential energy of a body placed at that point?

answer.model_answer_md: Gravitational potential is the potential energy per unit mass at the point (equal to $-GM/r$, with zero at infinity); its unit is J kg$^{-1}$. Potential energy $U = mV$ belongs to a particular body of mass $m$ there, while potential describes the point and is independent of the mass placed there.

questions.solution_md: V = U/m = −GM/r; unit J/kg.

marking_scheme.step: U = mV depends on the body; V depends only on the point

questions.stem_md: A satellite is lifted from the ground to a high orbit along two different routes. Explain why the work done against gravity is the same for both routes.

answer.model_answer_md: Gravity is a conservative force: the work it does depends only on the initial and final positions, not on the path, and over a closed path it is zero. The work done against gravity equals the gain in potential energy $U_f - U_i$, fixed by the end points alone.

questions.solution_md: Conservative force: work depends only on end points.

marking_scheme.step: Work = U_f − U_i, fixed by the end points

questions.stem_md: Derive the expression for the gravitational potential energy of a mass m at a distance r from the centre of the Earth (mass M), taking the potential energy to be zero at infinity.

answer.model_answer_md: An external agent moves $m$ in from infinity to $r$ at constant speed, applying a force equal and opposite to gravity, of magnitude $GMm/x^2$ directed away from $M$. The work done is $W = \int_{\infty}^{r} \dfrac{GMm}{x^2}\,dx = GMm\left[-\dfrac{1}{x}\right]_{\infty}^{r} = -\dfrac{GMm}{r}$. Since $U(\infty) = 0$, and gravity is conservative so that only the end points matter, this work is the potential energy: $U(r) = -\dfrac{GMm}{r}$.

questions.solution_md: Integrate the force from infinity: U = −GMm/r.

marking_scheme.step: Force on m at x is GMm/x² towards M
Work from ∞ to r by the external agent: integral of the force

questions.stem_md: The Moon has mass 7.35 × 10²² kg and radius 1.74 × 10⁶ m. Taking G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², find the speed needed to escape from the Moon’s surface, in km/s (ignore the Earth’s pull).
questions.solution_md: $v_e = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 \times 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 7.35 \times 10^{22}}{1.74 \times 10^6}} = \sqrt{5.63 \times 10^{6}} = 2374$ m/s $= 2.37$ km/s.

questions.stem_md: A satellite skims just above the surface of the Earth, so that its orbit radius is R = 6.4 × 10⁶ m. With g = 9.8 m/s², find its orbital speed, in km/s.
questions.solution_md: Gravity supplies the centripetal force: $m g = \dfrac{m v^2}{R}$, so $v = \sqrt{gR} = \sqrt{9.8 \times 6.4 \times 10^6} = 7920$ m/s $= 7.92$ km/s.

questions.stem_md: A satellite skims just above the Earth’s surface (R = 6.4 × 10⁶ m, g = 9.8 m/s²). Find the time it takes to complete one revolution, in minutes.
questions.solution_md: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{R}{g}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{6.4 \times 10^6}{9.8}} = 2\pi \times 808.1 = 5078$ s $= 84.6$ min.

questions.stem_md: An Earth-observation satellite is in a circular orbit 600 km above the Earth’s surface. Take G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², M = 6.0 × 10²⁴ kg and R = 6.4 × 10⁶ m. Find its orbital speed, in km/s.
questions.solution_md: The orbit radius is $r = R + h = 6.4 \times 10^6 + 6.0 \times 10^5 = 7.00 \times 10^{6}$ m. Then $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{r}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 6.0 \times 10^{24}}{7.0 \times 10^6}} = 7561$ m/s $= 7.56$ km/s.

questions.stem_md: A remote-sensing satellite moves in a circular orbit of radius 7.0 × 10⁶ m about the Earth (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², M = 6.0 × 10²⁴ kg). Find the time for one revolution, in minutes.

A 500 kg satellite is in a circular orbit of radius 7.0 × 10⁶ m about the Earth. With the potential energy zero at infinity, find its total mechanical energy, in GJ. Use G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻² and M = 6.0 × 10²⁴ kg. Give the sign.

questions.stem_md: A 500 kg satellite is moved from a circular orbit of radius 7.0 × 10⁶ m to a circular orbit of radius 1.0 × 10⁷ m about the Earth. Find the extra energy that must be supplied, in GJ (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², M = 6.0 × 10²⁴ kg).

answer.model_answer_md: The total energy $E = -GMm/2r$ decreases, so the orbit radius shrinks. Kinetic energy is $K = GMm/2r$, which grows as $r$ falls. The fall in potential energy is twice the fall in $E$, so gravity’s positive work exceeds the work lost to drag and the speed rises.

questions.solution_md: E decreases, r decreases, K = −E increases.

questions.stem_md: What does the negative sign of the total energy of an orbiting satellite tell us, and what is meant by its binding energy?

answer.model_answer_md: Negative total energy means the satellite is **bound**: it has less energy than a body at rest at infinity and cannot leave unaided. Its binding energy is the extra energy $|E| = GMm/2r$ that must be supplied to take it to infinity with zero speed.

questions.solution_md: Bound state; binding energy |E| = GMm/2r.

marking_scheme.step: Negative E: bound to the planet

questions.stem_md: Derive an expression for the escape speed from the surface of a planet of mass M and radius R, and show that it equals √(2gR). Evaluate it for the Earth (g = 9.8 m/s², R = 6.4 × 10⁶ m).

answer.model_answer_md: To escape, the body must just reach infinity with zero kinetic energy, where the potential energy is also zero, so its total energy at launch must be zero: $\tfrac{1}{2}mv_e^2 - \dfrac{GMm}{R} = 0$. This gives $v_e = \sqrt{2GM/R}$ and, with $GM = gR^2$, $v_e = \sqrt{2gR}$. For the Earth this is $\sqrt{2 \times 9.8 \times 6.4 \times 10^6} = 11200$ m/s $= 11.2$ km/s.

questions.solution_md: Total energy zero; GM = gR².

marking_scheme.step: Energy at the surface and at infinity set equal

questions.stem_md: A satellite circles the Earth at a height h above the surface. Derive expressions for its orbital speed and its period in terms of G, M, R and h.

answer.model_answer_md: The satellite’s orbit radius is $r = R + h$. Gravity alone supplies the centripetal force, so $\dfrac{GMm}{r^2} = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$ and the mass of the satellite cancels. The orbital speed is therefore $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{R+h}}$. One revolution covers a distance $2\pi r$ at speed $v$, so $T = \dfrac{2\pi r}{v} = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{(R+h)^3}{GM}}$, which does not depend on the satellite’s mass either.

questions.solution_md: Equate gravity and mv²/r.

questions.stem_md: (a) State Kepler’s law of orbits and law of periods. (b) A moon of mass m moves in a circular orbit of radius r about a planet of mass M. Derive the relation between its period T and r. (c) Phobos circles Mars in a nearly circular orbit of radius 9.4 × 10⁶ m with a period of 7.65 hours. Use G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻² to find the mass of Mars, in units of 10²³ kg.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Orbits:** each planet moves in an ellipse with the Sun at one focus. **Periods:** the square of the period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis.

(b) Gravity supplies the centripetal force: $\dfrac{GMm}{r^2} = m\omega^2 r$ with $\omega = 2\pi/T$, giving $T^2 = \dfrac{4\pi^2}{GM}\,r^3$.

(c) $T = 7.65 \times 3600 = 27540$ s. Then $M = \dfrac{4\pi^2 r^3}{G T^2} = \dfrac{4\pi^2 \times (9.4 \times 10^6)^3}{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times (27540)^2} = 6.48 \times 10^{23}$ kg. In units of $10^{23}$ kg: $M = 6.48$.

questions.solution_md: Statements; T² = 4π²r³/GM; M = 4π²r³/(GT²) ≈ 6.48 × 10²³ kg.

marking_scheme.step: Law of orbits and law of periods stated

questions.stem_md: (a) Derive the acceleration due to gravity at a height h above the surface of the Earth and show that it is approximately g(1 − 2h/R) for h much smaller than R. (b) Derive the acceleration due to gravity at a depth d below the surface, taking the Earth to be of uniform density. (c) Taking R = 6.4 × 10⁶ m, find the height and the depth at which g is 1.0% less than its surface value, in km.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) At height $h$ the distance from the centre is $R + h$: $g' = \dfrac{GM}{(R+h)^2} = g\left(1 + \dfrac{h}{R}\right)^{-2} \approx g\left(1 - \dfrac{2h}{R}\right)$ for $h \ll R$.

(b) At depth $d$ only the sphere of radius $R - d$ attracts; its mass is $M(R-d)^3/R^3$, so $g' = \dfrac{GM(R-d)}{R^3} = g\left(1 - \dfrac{d}{R}\right)$.

(c) For a fall of 1.0%: $\dfrac{2h}{R} = 0.010$ gives $h = 0.0050 \times 6.4 \times 10^6 = 3.20 \times 10^{4}$ m $= 32.0$ km; and $\dfrac{d}{R} = 0.010$ gives $d = 0.010 \times 6.4 \times 10^6 = 6.40 \times 10^{4}$ m $= 64.0$ km, twice as far.

marking_scheme.step: Only the inner sphere attracts at depth d

questions.stem_md: (a) Derive the expression for the gravitational potential energy of a mass m at distance r from the centre of the Earth, taking the zero at infinity. (b) Show that the increase of potential energy in raising m from the surface to a height h is mgRh/(R + h), and that it reduces to mgh for small h. (c) Find the least work needed to take a 1000 kg satellite from the Earth’s surface to infinity, in GJ (g = 9.8 m/s², R = 6.4 × 10⁶ m).

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The work done by an external agent in bringing $m$ slowly from infinity to $r$ is $\int_\infty^r \dfrac{GMm}{x^2}\,dx = -\dfrac{GMm}{r}$; with $U(\infty) = 0$ this is $U(r) = -\dfrac{GMm}{r}$.

(b) $\Delta U = GMm\left(\dfrac{1}{R} - \dfrac{1}{R+h}\right) = \dfrac{GMm\,h}{R(R+h)} = \dfrac{mgRh}{R+h}$ using $GM = gR^2$. For $h \ll R$, $R + h \approx R$ and $\Delta U \approx mgh$.

(c) Taking the satellite to infinity needs $-U(R) = \dfrac{GMm}{R} = mgR = 1000 \times 9.8 \times 6.4 \times 10^6 = 6.27 \times 10^{10}$ J $= 62.7$ GJ.

questions.solution_md: U = −GMm/r; ΔU = mgRh/(R + h) ≈ mgh; W = mgR = 62.7 GJ.

marking_scheme.step: Work from infinity to r by an external agent
ΔU = GMm h/(R(R + h)) = mgRh/(R + h)

questions.stem_md: (a) Derive the expression for the escape speed from the surface of a planet of mass M and radius R. (b) Derive the orbital speed of a satellite skimming the surface of the same planet and find the ratio of the two speeds. (c) A planet has M = 4.8 × 10²⁴ kg and R = 5.0 × 10⁶ m. Find both speeds, in km/s (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²).

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) For escape the total energy must be at least zero: $\tfrac{1}{2}mv_e^2 - \dfrac{GMm}{R} = 0$, so $v_e = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}}$.

(b) For a skimming orbit $\dfrac{mv_o^2}{R} = \dfrac{GMm}{R^2}$, so $v_o = \sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{R}}$ and $\dfrac{v_e}{v_o} = \sqrt{2}$.

(c) $v_e = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 \times 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 4.8 \times 10^{24}}{5.0 \times 10^6}} = 11320$ m/s $= 11.3$ km/s, and $v_o = \dfrac{v_e}{\sqrt{2}} = 8.00$ km/s.

questions.stem_md: (a) A satellite of mass m moves in a circular orbit of radius r about the Earth (mass M). Derive expressions for its kinetic energy, potential energy and total energy. (b) Explain the sign of the total energy and define the binding energy. (c) A 1000 kg satellite is in a circular orbit of radius 9.0 × 10⁶ m. Find K, U and E, in GJ (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², M = 6.0 × 10²⁴ kg).

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) From $\dfrac{mv^2}{r} = \dfrac{GMm}{r^2}$ we get $K = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = \dfrac{GMm}{2r}$. With zero at infinity $U = -\dfrac{GMm}{r}$, so $E = K + U = -\dfrac{GMm}{2r} = -K$.

(b) $E < 0$ means the satellite is bound to the Earth. The binding energy is $|E| = \dfrac{GMm}{2r}$, the least extra energy needed to free it.

(c) $K = \dfrac{GMm}{2r} = \dfrac{4.00 \times 10^{17}}{1.80 \times 10^{7}} = 2.22 \times 10^{10}$ J $= 22.2$ GJ; $U = -2K = -44.5$ GJ; $E = -22.2$ GJ.
